12662-four-girls-at-chautauqua:
Pansy's 1876 Four Girls at Chautauqua follows four young women to the famous lakeside assembly. Chapters run from introduced and the question discussed, through entering the current, Fairpoint, unrest, feasts and table talk. At evening time it shall be bright, fleeing, how the flitting ended, heart touches and Flossy at school follow.

Cross purposes, a new lesson, great men, war of words and getting ready to live close the tale. Pansy, author of Chautauqua Girls at Home, writes evangelical fiction for girls, earnest and warm. The novel shows Chautauqua as a place of study, song and conversion, where friendship and faith grow together by the lake.
15322-the-american-architect-and-buildin:
This January 11, 1890 number of The American Architect and Building News, volume twenty-seven, opens with a summary on its international edition, the influence of journals on architects' reputations, and publication irregularity. Death of architect Charles Keely, a move to end tariffs on art, and borrowed fire engines follow.

Notes on the Duke of Brunswick's monument at Geneva and an opening for American work round out the summary. The journal served builders and architects with news, criticism, and practice notes. Architecture historians will find the issue a crisp snapshot of the trade in 1890.
19690-apologia-pro-vita-sua:
John Henry Newman wrote this defense of his life and faith, published in London and New York. It answers Charles Kingsley's charges against him, first by exposing Kingsley's method of dispute, then by tracing Newman's own religious opinions from his youth to his move to Rome.

Newman is frank about his perplexity when old appeals to antiquity, once used for Anglican claims, seemed to fail him. The Apologia is both a personal history and a classic of English prose, and it made Newman's conversion intelligible to a wide public. Newman draws a broad line between actual belief and usage in Roman communion countries and her formal dogmas.
26946-the-defence-of-stonington-connecti:
Printed at Hartford in 1864, this small volume gathers the record of Stonington, Connecticut, holding off a British squadron from August 9 to 12, 1814. A handful of local volunteers, with just two working guns behind a low earthwork, drove the attackers off without losing a single life.

Inside are the muster roll of Captain William Potter's company, letters from Captain Amos Palmer, and Philip Freneau's poem on the battle. Together they preserve a War of 1812 action that the town marked each year, told mostly in the words of the men who stood there.
29554-an-ethnologist-s-view-of-history-a:
Daniel G. Brinton, professor of American archaeology at the University of Pennsylvania, gave this address before the New Jersey Historical Society at Trenton on January 28, 1896. Printed in Philadelphia that year, it asks how a student of peoples should view history. Many answers, Brinton warns, are offered with equal confidence, yet they clash strangely with each other.

Brinton urges a science of history grounded in ethnology: the study of peoples, their growth, and their traits. The address speaks to historians as a friendly challenge from a neighboring field. Readers of anthropology and historiography will find a clear, period statement of how one science hoped to guide another.
30621-ancient-art-of-the-province-of-chi:
William H. Holmes writes Ancient Art of the Province of Chiriqui, Colombia, a Bureau of American Ethnology study of objects, graves, and peoples. Contents move from introduction, geography, literature, and peoples to cemeteries, graves, human remains, placing of relics, and objects of art.

Stone work opens the art sections, with pictured rocks and columns, leading into a detailed survey of Chiriqui craft. Holmes, working from field and museum evidence, describes forms, materials, and burial practice with care. The study serves archaeologists, students, and readers interested in ancient American art and the peoples who made it.
32768-the-story-of-chautauqua:
Jesse Lyman Hurlbut tells the history of Chautauqua, the lakeside summer institution founded by Lewis Miller and John Heyl Vincent, published by Putnam in 1921 with fifty illustrations. Hurlbut defends the book with testimony from governors, senators, educators, and preachers who called Chautauqua the common people's college.

Chapters follow the assemblies, the Hall of Philosophy, and the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle, whose executive secretary Kate Fisher Kimball served from youth until her death in 1917. The narrative closes with crowds, banners, and white handkerchiefs greeting their leader at the pier, a portrait of popular education at its most festive.
3396-literary-boston-as-i-knew-it-from-l:
William Dean Howells remembers literary Boston as he knew it in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Among his fellow passengers on the train from New York to Boston was Samuel Bowles of the Springfield Republican. Howells went to begin work there in 1866 as assistant editor of the Atlantic Monthly. Bowles had created, in a subordinate city, a journal of metropolitan importance.

Howells had met Bowles in Venice several years earlier, and the train ride renewed the acquaintance. The memoir that follows maps Boston's literary world through its people: editors, poets, and publishers met on trains, in offices, and at dinner tables. Readers get the Atlantic's Boston from inside, as a young Ohioan saw it on arrival and learned it by living there.
6321-the-naturalist-in-nicaragua:
Thomas Belt, introduced by Anthony Belt, lands at Greytown on Nicaragua's Caribbean shore and notes the San Juan river, its silting harbour, and its dangerous bar. Sharks patrol, Columbus is recalled, and the town's trade and health draw comment. Wild fruits, plants, parrots, toucans, tanagers, butterflies, and beetles fill his lists, with mimetic forms, alligators, and a boy drowned at Blewfields among the harder notes.

Up the San Juan, Belt studies palms, plantations, and the Colorado river, watches foraging ants hunt and attack other ants' nests, and weighs reasoning powers in ants against mammals. Motmots, ant thrushes, and birds' nests preserved from ants give the book its close observation. Belt writes as a field naturalist, patient with small facts, and his Nicaragua becomes a living laboratory of mimicry, instinct, and river life.
8233-the-world-english-bible-web-joshua:
Joshua, in the World English Bible, opens after the death of Moses, servant of Yahweh, when Yahweh speaks to Joshua son of Nun: Moses is dead, so arise. Cross the Jordan with all this people to the land given to Israel, every place the sole of your foot treads. From the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the great sea. No man will stand before Joshua all his life, as God was with Moses, so he will be with him. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book tells the conquest.

The modern version keeps the campaigns, the crossing, Jericho, and the division of the land in brisk narrative prose. Joshua here reads as a story of succession and promise kept. For readers continuing from Deuteronomy, this rendering carries the history forward without a change of voice.
875-the-duchess-of-padua:
Oscar Wilde wrote this early verse play about Guido Ferranti, a young man sworn to avenge his father's death on Simone Gesso, Duke of Padua. Guido wins the love of Beatrice, the Duke's wife and Duchess of Padua, and murder, passion, and betrayal follow. Cardinals, lords, and soldiers crowd the court.

Wilde wrote the play in blank verse before his comedies made him famous, and its rhetoric is lush and romantic. The plot turns on revenge grown into love, and on a duchess caught between duty and heart. The play shows Wilde learning his stagecraft, and it still interests readers of his early, tragic mode.
8911-explorations-in-australia-the-journ:
John McDouall Stuart's journals record his explorations in Australia during 1858 through 1862, when he fixed the centre of the continent and crossed it successfully from sea to sea. William Hardman edited the journals from Stuart's manuscript, with maps, a photographic portrait, and twelve wood engravings by George French Angas from sketches made on the expeditions. A second edition of 1865 notes that Stuart had since arrived in England, where the Geographical Society heard his account.

Stuart's spare daily entries track water, feed, horses, sickness, and the slow push north through desert that defeated others. His crossing opened the route for the overland telegraph and for settlement, at great cost to his health. Readers of exploration will find a classic Australian journal: unadorned, stubborn, and heroic in its refusal to turn back, and a foundation document of the continent's interior history.
apologia-pro-vita-sua: John Henry Newman writes his Apologia pro vita sua, a defence of his life and religious path, in parts that trace his journey to Rome. The work answers charges against his honesty, recounting his Oxford years and conversion. Newman's Apologia stands as a classic of spiritual autobiography in English. Its calm candour won even former foes over.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chihuahua: A short entry on the Diocese of Chihuahua, which covers the Mexican state of that name in the north of the country. Its population of about 327,000 is mostly Indians and mestizos, people of mixed Indian and Spanish descent. Erected in 1891, the diocese has had two bishops: José de Jesús Ortiz, promoted to Guadalajara's archbishopric, and Nicholas Perez Gavilan. A few figures sketch its life: a seminary with 50 students preparing for the priesthood, 42 parishes, and 64 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comayagua:
Feliciano Herrera's entry covers the Diocese of Comayagua, suffragan to Guatemala. It takes in the whole Republic of Honduras in Central America, about 46,250 square miles. Its population in 1902, apart from uncivilized Indians, stood at 684,400, mostly baptized Catholics. It also takes in islets of the Bay of Honduras: Ruatan, Bonacca, Utila, Barbareta, and Moret. The land runs mountainous, with fertile plains and plateaux, and roads are few.

A railroad from Puerto Cortez to La Pimienta, sixty miles long, was meant to reach the Pacific. Mineral wealth runs great, and banana trade pays well. The inland climate stays healthy, though fevers haunt the low coast. Tegucigalpa, the capital, held 17,000 people. Franciscans came first as missionaries, though records of their work have vanished. Between 1878 and 1880 a president imposed by Guatemala seized church goods anew, and scattered villages still strain to support priests and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congrua:
William Fanning's entry defines congrua, or congrua portio, the canonical term for the lowest proper yearly income of a cleric. It sometimes carries the same sense as competency. Benefices bore many charges, so ecclesiastical authority decreed that the holder's sustenance come first and foremost, with a minimum revenue below which income must not fall. Need grew sharpest where benefices stood incorporated with monasteries or collegiate churches.

Curates of such incorporated benefices very often received only one-sixteenth of the revenue. Ordinances followed to remedy the abuse, reserving a decent subsistence to the person holding cure of souls. The Council of Trent took up determination in Session XXI, chapter four, on reform. Later canonists and handbooks, from Ferraris and Vering to Buchberger, carried the question through Austrian and general church law, keeping the cleric's minimum living at the center of benefice administration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josue-joshua:
Josue, or Joshua, was Moses' successor who led Israel into the promised land. Chosen by Moses and confirmed by God, he took command after Moses' death and crossed the Jordan on dry ground. His book, the sixth of the Old Testament, falls into two parts: the conquest of Canaan and the allotment of land to the tribes.

The conquest tells of Jericho's fallen walls, the defeat at Ai through Achan's crime, victories over southern and northern kings, and the sparing of Rahab's family. The division allots territory tribe by tribe, ending with Josue's farewell and death. Early Fathers called the book Jesus Nave, seeing in Josue a type of Jesus, the ship in which the world is saved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mantua:
Mantua was a diocese in Lombardy, seated on the Mincio River. The river rings the city and forms swampy lowlands. Those marshes helped make Mantua Italy's strongest fortress, though they also bred disease. Its cathedral was the ancient church of Saints Peter and Paul, and its secular glories included the Palazzo della Ragione and the Ducal Palace, begun in 1302.

Famous sons included Virgil and Sordello among its poets. Tradition says St Longinus brought the Gospel, and synods met there in 827, 1053, and 1064. Once suffragan to Aquileia, it came directly under the Holy See in 1452, then under Ferrara in 1803. Its bishops and buildings, its fortress strength, and its place in church disputes fill an entry that joins town history to diocesan history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marsilius-of-:
Marsilius of Padua was a physician and theologian, born about 1270 and dead about 1342. He served the emperor's army, studied medicine at Padua, finished at Paris, and became Paris university rector before December 1312.

His state theory gave all church power to the community and the emperor, its chief agent, with no limit on lay state rights. Peter, he said, held no more power than other apostles, and may never have reached Rome. The pope could only call a general council, which stood above him, and his decrees bound no one beyond council decisions. John XXII condemned five of his propositions in October 1327 and excommunicated him. Marsilius then marched to Italy with Louis of Bavaria, who crowned himself by the Roman people's syndic, deposed John, set up Peter of Corbara, and made Marsilius imperial vicar. Abandoned by Louis in 1336, he died about 1342.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicaragua:
Nicaragua, republic and diocese, is a Central American republic between Honduras and Costa Rica, the Pacific and the Caribbean, covering 49,200 square miles with about 600,000 people. Most inhabitants are aborigines, negroes or of mixed blood, with pure European descent under 1,500. A single chamber of thirty-six members, elected for six years, holds legislative power, and a president, also six years, rules through nine cabinet ministers.

A deep depression parallel to the Pacific coast holds volcanoes, including Monotombo at 7,000 feet, and great lakes Managua and Nicaragua, or Cocibolca. The country takes its name from the latter, 92 miles long and up to 40 wide, named for Nicarao, the chief ruling round Lake Cocibolca when Davila's Spaniards explored in 1522. Spanish until 1822, then part of the Central American federation until 1839, its church history, bishops and missions complete the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-padua:
Padua is a diocese in northern Italy, its city set on a fertile plain crossed by the Bacchiglione River, its streets mostly lined with colonnades. Splendid above its churches stands il Santo, the basilica of Saint Anthony, begun in 1232 in mixed Romanesque and Byzantine style, with seven cupolas and three naves. Donatello's bronze crucifix crowns the high altar, and paintings by Mantegna, Veronese, and Tiepolo fill the church.

Santa Giustina, rebuilt in 1502, carries eight cupolas and fourteen side chapels, beside a Benedictine monastery from the ninth century where a noted reform began. The cathedral fell in the earthquake of 1117 and rose again under Michelangelo, who finished only part. The entry follows the diocese's bishops, its university fame, and its churches through later centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anthony-of:
St. Anthony of Padua was a Franciscan wonder-worker, born at Lisbon in 1195. He died on 13 June 1231. This entry follows a boy baptized Ferdinand, whose later genealogy is uncertain. Fifteenth-century writers made his father Martin Bouillon, a descendant of Godfrey de Bouillon, and his mother Theresa Tavejra, a descendant of Froila I. The entry warns that all certainly known is that his parents were noble, powerful, and God-fearing, living near Lisbon cathedral when he was born.

Educated in the cathedral school, Ferdinand joined the Canons Regular of St. Augustine at St. Vincent outside Lisbon at fifteen, in 1210. Two years later he moved to avoid distraction from visiting relatives and friends. The entry follows him from Augustinian canon to Franciscan friar, preacher, and saint, whose fame as a thaumaturgist spread across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-felicitas:
Perpetua and Felicitas died at Carthage on 7 March 203, with three companions, Revocatus, Saturus, and Saturninus. This entry draws on a genuine account written at the time, one of the most moving martyrdom records of the ancient Church. Perpetua was a young married lady of noble birth, while Felicitas was her slave.

Severus had banned conversion to Christianity, so the five catechumens were seized, baptized, and jailed. Prison scenes follow: the dark cell, a pagan father's pleas, a nursing infant, and visions seen by Perpetua and Saturus. A later hand added the execution itself. Their story remains a window into the North African Church under persecution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Padua's university dates, by some anonymous chronicles, from 1222, when part of Bologna's studium, professors and students together, withdrew to Padua. The claim that Frederick II moved Bologna's studium to Padua in 1241 is groundless, the entry insists. Yet law professors already taught at Padua before the migration, such as Gerardus Pomadellus about 1165, later Bishop of Padua, and his predecessor Bishop Carzo, called a doctor of sacred canons.

A contract proposed by the commune of Vercelli in 1228 shows law, dialectics, medicine, and grammar all taught at Padua. Students split into four nations: French, Italian, German, and Provençal. The entry follows the university's privileges, its student nations, and its famed medical school, giving a compact history of a school born from a secession. It grew into one of Italy's great universities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-of-cap:
Victor of Capua was a sixth-century bishop known almost solely from his epitaph, preserved though his tomb has vanished. The inscription states that his thirteen-year episcopate ended in April 554, and its authenticity and dates admit of no doubt. He is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 17 October as conspicuous for learning and holiness.

His writings survive only in fragments, yet show a devoted student of wide learning. Best known is the Codex Fuldensis, one of the oldest Vulgate manuscripts, prepared under his direction and revised by his own hand, in which a gospel harmony replaces the four separate gospels. Victor doubted whether his harmony matched Tatian's Diatessaron; modern research shows it was a Latin harmony drawn up about AD 500, substituting Jerome's Vulgate for Tatian's Greek.

doe-osti-3365797-waveform-simulation-fra: Scientists who simulate waveforms — the wiggles of sound, seismic shaking, or electromagnetic signals — need good software. This user manual with tutorials introduces a waveform simulation framework and teaches newcomers how to run it. Step-by-step examples lower the bar for doing serious wave science.
doe-osti-3374778-generalized-integral-bo: Air flowing over a wing follows curving paths, and engineers need equations that follow along. This paper generalizes the integral boundary layer equations into streamline curvilinear coordinates — math shaped to the flow itself. The result is a cleaner toolkit for predicting drag and heat on fast vehicles.

explorations-in-australia-the-journals-o:
Stuart's Explorations in Australia prints his journals from the years 1858 to 1862. John McDouall Stuart fixed the centre of the continent in those years. He then crossed Australia from sea to sea. William Hardman edited the journals from Stuart's own manuscript.

This second edition is dated 1865. It adds maps, a photographic portrait, and twelve engravings by George French Angas. The editor's preface ranks Stuart among Australia's most important explorers. Stuart first gained experience in 1844 under Captain Sturt, the preface notes. A note to this edition records his naming of Alexandra Land. The journals give day-by-day travel through harsh interior country. They document water, terrain, and party hardship in plain terms.
four-girls-at-chautauqua:
Pansy brings four girls to the Chautauqua assembly, where lectures and lake air mix with spiritual unrest. Ruth, Marion, and Flossy are introduced in the opening chapters, and the question of staying or flitting is discussed early. Fairpoint, feasts, and table talk fill the grounds.

Flossy declares that nothing could tempt her to leave Chautauqua for Saratoga just now, and will not say why. Ruth flees in vexation to the trees outside the tent, a new phase in her character. Marion sets herself to restore the peace. Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, published the novel in 1876.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Nicaraugua_Nica: Brian Barger of United Press International reported that an Iran-Contra figure had hidden a man wanted in a plane bombing. The story belongs to the Iran-Contra affair's long tail, when the scandal's side plots kept surfacing in the press. The file preserves Barger's headline and byline under a Nicaragua heading. It does not name the figure or the fugitive in the evidence given, so the story's details cannot be summarized here.
literary-boston-as-i-knew-it-from-litera:
William Dean Howells recalls his arrival in Boston in 1866. He came to serve as assistant editor of the Atlantic Monthly. Samuel Bowles of the Springfield Republican shared his train ride. Bowles had earlier suffered cruel insomnia from newspaper overwork.

Bowles delighted in the drama of a young Ohio newspaperman's rise. A western novice would now share the Atlantic's destinies. Howells doubts such a fact would move anyone today. The West has since flooded the East with authorship, he writes. Scarcely an hour of sleep in twenty-four marked Bowles's suffering. Venice had hosted their earlier meeting years before this train ride.
nasa-tm-19650025634-nasa-flight-research:
William E Gray Jr, head of a Flight Research Center branch at Edwards, described a handling-qualities program for small private aircraft in April 1964. He spoke at a general aviation design meeting in Wichita, Kansas. Handling qualities are how an aircraft feels and responds to its pilot. Small aircraft had rarely received the formal testing given to military types.

A set program brings test pilots and clear standards to that work. Poor handling in a light aircraft is a safety issue for ordinary owners. Gray sets out what the center's program did and why it mattered. The paper shows flight research reaching beyond rockets and jets, into everyday flying.
podcast-joerogan-D_ZGWj_38uA:
RZA, the founder and producer of the Wu-Tang Clan, sits for episode 2490 of the Joe Rogan Experience. RZA shaped one of hip-hop's greatest groups and built a second career in film. His talks tend to mix street history with the philosophy he has studied for decades.

He and Rogan move from the Clan's early days to chess, kung fu films, and the Eastern thought RZA folded into his music. Rogan draws out stories about the group's rise and the discipline behind it. The episode is a reflective session with a man who treats art, faith, and business as one practice.
podcast-tuckercarlson-cWpNSMsmGUA:
Journalist Glenn Greenwald joins Tucker Carlson for war updates and a look homeward. For two weeks, Carlson says, viewers watched the joint war on Iran. He warns that rights at home shrink while eyes stay abroad.

He notes that America, Europe, and allied nations have all clamped down. Greenwald weighs false flag claims and media framing. The title calls Israel's leader desperate for power. The talk ties foreign war to domestic control. Listeners get two veteran skeptics reading the same events and reaching a shared, grim view. Both treat free speech as the core issue.
tanakh-jps-1917-joshua:
Joshua is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's English version of 1917. It begins after the death of Moses, when the Lord speaks to Joshua son of Nun, who had served as Moses' aide.

Joshua is told to rise and lead all the people across the Jordan into the land sworn to their fathers. The bounds run from the desert and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the Great Sea. God pledges never to fail him, and urges him to be strong and hold fast to the law. Readers follow the entry into Canaan, its battles, and the sharing of land among the tribes.
the-american-architect-and-building-news: One weekly issue is present in contents form: The American Architect and Building News, volume 27, number 733, dated January 11, 1890, copyrighted by Ticknor and Company of Boston. Its summary weighs support for an international edition and a drive to end the tariff on works of art. Listed pieces cover civil and domestic building and a letter from Paris. Other pieces treat loss of power by heat radiation, the cost of a small museum, and burial reform. Plates show houses and churches at home and abroad.
the-duchess-of-padua: Oscar Wilde's play The Duchess of Padua, in a fifth edition from Methuen, is present here only as title matter and a cast list. Simone Gesso, Duke of Padua, and Beatrice his wife head the cast. A cardinal, courtiers, young Guido Ferranti, an old count, and Hugo the headsman fill the roll. The scene is Padua. No play text appears in these pages.
the-naturalist-in-nicaragua:
Thomas Belt's The Naturalist in Nicaragua is introduced, in this Dent and Dutton printing, by his relative Anthony Belt. The introduction quotes Charles Darwin's judgement from the Life and Letters edited by Francis Darwin. Reading Belt in 1874 gave Darwin great pleasure, and he wrote to Sir Joseph Hooker calling it the best of all natural history journals ever published.

Belt, the introduction explains, was an engineer by profession, so his observations in Nicaragua and elsewhere came from his leisure hours. His book is praised as direct and vivid, full of description and suggestive discussion. Two mottos head the volume: a Latin confession that the writer knows only that he knows nothing, and Everyman's promise to go with the reader and be his guide.
the-world-english-bible-web-joshua:
Book six in the World English Bible, Joshua, begins right after Moses' death. God speaks to Joshua, son of Nun and Moses' aide. Moses my servant is dead, God says. Now Joshua must lead Israel across the Jordan. Every place his foot treads is promised to them. Their border will stretch to the Euphrates and the great sea.

No one will withstand Joshua all his days, God promises. God vows to be with him as with Moses. Strength and courage are commanded repeatedly. The land sworn to their fathers awaits conquest. Readers move from wandering to settlement. Leadership passes, and a new generation takes the promise.
